p: The field north of Gettysburg was quiet when Iverson's four North Carolina regiments stepped off. They moved in perfect alignment — a textbook advance that would have drawn admiration on a parade ground. No skirmishers preceded them. No one had scouted the stone wall ahead.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Behind that wall, Baxter's Union brigade lay flat in the grass, waiting. The 12th Massachusetts, 83rd New York, 97th New York, 88th Pennsylvania, 90th Pennsylvania — all pressed close to the ground, rifles ready.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Iverson's men had covered perhaps half the distance when Baxter's soldiers rose up behind the wall and fired.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: The volley came simultaneously along a front of several hundred yards. Iverson's regiments were struck in the flank — the wall ran parallel to their line of advance. Men fell in rows exactly as they had been marching, in perfect military alignment, because there had been no time to break formation before the fire swept through them.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: About 500 men fell in the first minutes. Not wounded — fell, shot, lying in the grass in the same lines they had been marching in.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Iverson, watching from behind, reportedly believed his men had surrendered. He sent word to Rodes that his brigade had thrown up the white flag in dishonor. It was not true. His men were not surrendering. They were dying.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: When Union soldiers advanced after the battle to bury the dead, they found the bodies lying in such perfect order that little digging was needed. They buried them where they fell, in shallow trenches that followed the line of the advance.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: The slight depressions of those graves are visible at Oak Ridge today.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Iverson was relieved of command shortly after the battle. He was never given another brigade.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: The charge of Gordon's Georgia brigade had swept everything before it. When it was over, when the Union line on Barlow's Knoll had collapsed and the Confederates were pursuing the broken XI Corps south toward Gettysburg, John Gordon rode over the ground his men had taken.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Gordon and Barlow”, paragraph 1 of 11

p: He found a Union general lying among the dead, shot through the body and left behind in the rout. The man was barely conscious.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Gordon and Barlow”, paragraph 2 of 11

p: Gordon dismounted. He raised the officer's head, gave him water from his own canteen, tried to make him comfortable. He asked if there was anything he could do.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Gordon and Barlow”, paragraph 3 of 11

p: The dying man — it was General Francis Barlow, commanding the First Division of the XI Corps — said he did not expect to live. He asked Gordon, if it were possible, to find his wife and tell her where he had fallen.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Gordon and Barlow”, paragraph 4 of 11

p: Gordon promised. He had the general moved to a shaded spot and left a Confederate soldier to care for him. Then he rejoined the pursuit.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Gordon and Barlow”, paragraph 5 of 11

p: Barlow did not die. Against all expectation, he recovered — slowly, painfully — and returned to command. He served through the rest of the war. He became one of the best Union division commanders at the Overland Campaign.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Gordon and Barlow”, paragraph 6 of 11

p: After the war, Gordon heard a rumor that Barlow had died. Barlow heard a rumor that Gordon had died. They never sought each other out.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Gordon and Barlow”, paragraph 7 of 11
